title: Restoring a Sun-Damaged Wood Fence in Alachua
description: Gray, splintering fence boards can often be saved. How to clean, brighten, repair, and stain a sun-damaged wood fence in Alachua County's climate.
h1: Treating a Sun-Damaged Wood Fence in Alachua County
heroIntro: A gray, rough fence is usually weathered on the surface, not finished. With cleaning, a brightener, a few new pickets, and a penetrating stain, most fences can be brought back before replacement makes sense.
excerpt: Gray, splintering fence boards can often be saved. How to clean, brighten, repair, and stain a sun-damaged wood fence in Alachua County.

secondary: how often to stain a fence in florida
questions: Can a gray weathered fence be restored?
What is the best stain for a wood fence in Florida?
How often should a fence be stained in Florida?

sections.h2: What sun does to fence boards
body: Wood is made of cellulose fibers held together by lignin. Ultraviolet light breaks down lignin at the surface, which loosens the fibers and turns the wood silver-gray. Rain then washes away the degraded material, leaving a rough, fuzzy surface. In Alachua County, where fences often run along open yards and pasture with no shade, that process is fast, and pressure-treated pine fencing can go gray within a season or two if left unprotected.

The good news is that the graying is usually only skin deep. Beneath a thin layer of damaged fibers, the wood is often sound. Stain applied over the gray layer will not penetrate or bond well, so the damaged surface has to be removed first.

sections.h2: Assess the fence before you restore it
body: Walk the fence line with a screwdriver and check:
bullets: Posts at ground level. Push and probe; soft or wobbly posts are rotting and need replacement or bracing.
Pickets and rails for splits, cupping, or soft areas, especially near the ground and around sprinkler zones.
Loose or rusted fasteners. Replace with exterior-rated, corrosion-resistant screws or nails.
Mildew, algae, or green growth on the shaded side.
Any old paint or solid stain, which changes how the fence must be prepared.

body: Plan the work for a dry stretch; the wood must be clean and dry before staining. Fall and spring are generally the best seasons in North Central Florida.
bullets: Replace failed pickets and posts first, so new wood can be cleaned and stained along with the rest.
Clean with a wood cleaner to kill mildew and lift dirt. Apply with a pump sprayer and scrub with a stiff brush where needed.
Rinse gently. If you use a pressure washer, use a wide fan tip at low pressure and keep it moving; too much pressure gouges the soft spring wood and raises fibers.
Apply a wood brightener, typically oxalic acid based, to restore the wood's color and neutralize the cleaner. Rinse thoroughly.
Let the fence dry for at least a couple of dry days, then lightly sand any rough or fuzzy areas.
Apply a penetrating semi-transparent stain with a pump sprayer, brush, or roller, and back-brush to work it into the grain. Avoid puddles and lap marks.

sections.h2: Choosing a stain for Florida sun
body: For fences, a penetrating semi-transparent stain is usually the best choice. It soaks into the wood rather than forming a film, so it does not peel; it gradually weathers and can be refreshed with another coat after cleaning. The pigment in semi-transparent stain provides UV protection that clear sealers lack, so a clear finish will not prevent graying for long in our sun.

Solid stains and paint look more uniform and hide mismatched boards, but they form a film that can peel and requires more prep to maintain. Whichever you choose, apply it to all accessible faces and, if possible, the cut ends of pickets, where moisture enters the wood first. New pressure-treated lumber often needs to dry for some time before it will accept stain; a few drops of water that bead instead of soaking in tell you it is not ready.
Maintenance is what decides whether you are restoring the fence again in two years or simply refreshing it.
bullets: Re-stain every two to three years in full sun, or whenever water no longer beads on the surface.
Adjust sprinklers so they do not spray the fence, and keep mulch and soil from piling up against boards.
Trim vines and shrubs that hold moisture against the fence.
Clean off mildew on the shaded side once a year with a gentle wood cleaner.
Tighten or replace loose fasteners before boards warp.

sections.h2: Mistakes that shorten a fence restoration
body: Most fence finishes that fail early do so for one of a few reasons. Staining too soon after washing is the most common: wood that feels dry on the surface may still be damp inside, and stain applied over moisture will not penetrate and can blotch or peel. Give it at least a couple of dry days, longer after heavy rain. Applying too much stain is the second; semi-transparent stains are meant to soak in, and excess that sits on the surface stays tacky, collects pollen and dirt, and can flake. Wipe or back-brush any puddles.

Spraying on a windy day sends stain onto cars, siding, and a neighbor's property, so mask nearby surfaces and pick a calm morning. Finally, chlorine bleach is not a substitute for a wood cleaner. It can damage wood fibers and kill plants without removing the gray layer as effectively as an oxygenated wood cleaner followed by a brightener. Protect plants from any cleaner by wetting them down before and after.

sections.h2: When replacement is the better choice
body: Restoration makes sense when most posts are sound and only some pickets need replacing. If posts are rotting along much of the fence line, boards are badly split and cupped, or the fence leans, replacement may be the better investment. Our article on signs of wood rot explains how to spot rot early, and the same principles apply to fence posts. A middle option is replacing the posts and rails while keeping good pickets, or rebuilding only the worst sections and staining the whole run so old and new boards blend over time.

faqs.q: Can I stain over a gray fence without cleaning it?
faqs.a: No. The gray layer is damaged wood fiber that stain cannot bond to. Clean and brighten the wood, let it dry, and sand rough areas before staining.

faqs.q: How often should a wood fence be stained in Florida?
faqs.a: Fences in full sun typically need a fresh coat of semi-transparent stain every two to three years. When water stops beading on the surface, it is time.

faqs.q: Should I use paint or stain on a wood fence?
faqs.a: Penetrating semi-transparent stain is usually the better option because it soaks in and does not peel. Paint and solid stains form a film that can peel and needs more maintenance.

faqs.q: Can I pressure wash my fence?
faqs.a: Yes, but carefully. Use low pressure and a wide fan tip, keep the wand moving, and let the cleaner do most of the work. High pressure can gouge and splinter the wood.
